name: VARoleAdvisorWorkoutProgramFit

custom.system_prompt: Ryan wants to get back into consistent training after a lazy few months but is stuck between a demanding six-day program he found online and something more modest. He asks Sigma to help him pick an approach he'll actually stick to, not the technically optimal one.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.tts_prompt: Warm but practical, no lecturing tone

sound_effects_config.prompt: Apartment living room in the evening, quiet, occasional street sound through a cracked window

initial_prompt: Generate a scene where Ryan, a software engineer, is deciding between a demanding six-day training program he found online and a more modest three-day routine. He asks Sigma for help. Sigma asks about his actual available time, current routine, equipment access, and tolerance for tracking, then helps him see that a technically optimal program he can't sustain is worse than a realistic one. Keep every line short and natural, one or two spoken sentences — the opening line already addresses Sigma directly instead of thinking aloud alone first.

user1.name: Ryan
user1.tts_prompt: Relaxed and easygoing, casual evening tone

variations.context: Solo evening decision about which training program to actually commit to

setting.mood: Motivated but wary of over-promising to himself
setting.relationship_dynamic: Individual reasoning out loud after a stretch of inactivity
setting.background: Ryan has started and abandoned a few fitness plans before; this time he wants to pick something realistic
setting.conversation_style: Casual, self-aware, occasionally joking about past failed attempts

scenario_template.topic: Ryan addresses Sigma directly, folding his temptation toward the six-day program and his doubt about sustaining it into one short question — e.g. 'Sigma, I found this six-day program and I'm tempted, but I've bailed on stuff like this before. Can you help me figure out what I can actually stick to?' One short turn, straight to Sigma.
scenario_template.mood: Direct, a little sheepish about his track record

scenario_template.topic: Sigma asks about realistic available time, current routine, equipment, and desired pace
scenario_template.note: Ryan's answers should reveal a real schedule conflict — e.g. he can honestly commit to three sessions, not six.

scenario_template.topic: Sigma reframes the choice around sustainability rather than theoretical optimality. Sigma gives ONE clear recommendation in one or two short sentences — not a list of every alternative's requirements. The user's reaction is measured, not instant enthusiasm — a hedge, a practical worry, or lukewarm acceptance is more natural than immediate excitement.
scenario_template.note: Something like: a technically optimal six-day program he abandons in three weeks is worse than a three-day plan he actually finishes.

scenario_template.topic: Ryan commits to the more modest, sustainable plan with some relief. One short line only. Keep this grounded — voice at least one lingering doubt or hedge (e.g. 'we'll see', 'hope this actually sticks this time') rather than sounding fully convinced and upbeat.
scenario_template.mood: Relieved, a little amused at himself
scenario_template.note: Short closing beat — he jokes about finally being honest with himself about his schedule.

user1.name: Ryan
user1.role: Software engineer trying to restart consistent training. Tempted by an ambitious program but has a track record of abandoning overambitious plans. Casual, self-aware, responsive to a sustainability-focused reframing. Speaks in short natural sentences — never recites a list of every option's pros and cons in one breath. Reacts realistically, not with instant enthusiasm — voices at least a little hesitation, a practical worry, or partial reluctance before or even after agreeing; agreement is provisional, not a full conversion to positivity.

assistant.name: Sigma
assistant.role: Advisor. Elicits actual available time, routine, and equipment before recommending a training approach. Explicitly frames sustainability against theoretical optimality rather than praising the most demanding option. Keeps each turn to one short point — never lists every alternative's pros and cons in a single turn.

conversation_structure: The opening line already addresses Sigma directly — there is no separate solo turn thinking through the dilemma out loud beforehand.
The tension is between an ambitious plan and a sustainable one, not between two arbitrary programs
Sigma asks about realistic constraints before recommending anything
The resolution favors match-to-life over theoretical optimality, stated explicitly
Every line is one or two short spoken sentences — no long recited monologues enumerating every option's pros and cons.

Human reactions stay realistic and imperfect — hedged agreement, lingering doubt, or one partner less convinced than the other are more natural than universal enthusiasm and a perfectly neat resolution.
assistant_behavior: Sigma does not simply endorse the most demanding program
Sigma asks concrete questions about time and routine before advising
The final decision is framed as the user's own, informed choice
Sigma's own turns stay short too — one clear point per turn, not a paragraph listing every alternative.
